HEADLINE: MODERN MANNERS
TEXT:
Trends China's nouveau riche are flocking to etiquette classes to help them navigate high society in London, New York and Paris, writes Michael Smith.

Jacqueline Tang believes it is never too late to improve oneself. Today, the distinguished pianist and Shanghai socialite is learning how to rise from a velvet sofa with a book balanced precariously on her head.

Two other elegantly-dressed women are looking on, sipping tea and clapping politely at the completion of each graceful ascent. Tang laughs nervously but never loses her composure, somehow standing up straight with hands clasped demurely in the lap of her electric blue gown. She is also being taught how NOT to sit down.

"You should sit down and stand up with your back straight, not with your bum in the air and face to the ground," her Parisian-born teacher Guillaume Rue de Bernadac says from the sidelines, delivering instructions in Mandarin, French and English.

The table is heaving with expensive crockery, silver teapots, dainty sandwiches, scones and macaroons. We are in the luxurious Salon de Ville tearoom at the Waldorf Astoria overlooking Shanghai's famous Bund. Classical music wafts through the room. The afternoon's lessons, which cover everything from how to cross your legs to where to place your tea cup, are only just beginning.

The scene is a modern Chinese twist on My Fair Lady. Tang and her classmates are among thousands of affluent Chinese women taking up classes where they learn everything from deportment to dining etiquette and public speaking. For Tang, who often spends time mingling with the upper echelons of society in Europe and the United States, it is a necessary step in the evolution of China's newly-minted middle classes where she says good manners have failed to keep pace with the bank accounts of the country's nouveau riche.

"It is a reflection of your level of education. If you chew loudly people will say, 'This is a low-class person, he has nothing but money.' As China becomes richer people are starting to recognise that," says Tang, a piano professor at the Shanghai Conservatory of Music, who judges at international competitions in Italy and Spain.

"Everyone appreciates beauty but a beautiful face is just part of that. You can have a beautiful rose but you need a good vase to go with the flower. I bring my daughter to lessons. She is 15. But they are good for men too, not just just the ladies."

Tang is just one of thousands of well-heeled women in China taking etiquette classes designed to help them navigate high-society in New York, London and Paris. There are hundreds of Swiss-style finishing schools taking in debutantes across China, many of them locally run with various levels of legitimacy, as well as government-sponsored colleges taking a less Western-influenced approach.

The trend is a reflection of the dramatic social changes sweeping China. While the country's booming economy has created a new generation of wealthy elite, many have had little exposure to Western culture or international travel.

While formal manners are nothing new in China, particularly among the upper-classes in cities like Shanghai during the 1920s, the country was effectively closed off for six decades during Mao Zedong's Cultural Revolution. During this troubled period, etiquette was seen as bourgeois and discouraged.

Rue de Bernadac, one of China's most sought-after etiquette coaches, says while his clients want to adapt to these changes it does not necessarily mean they want to shed their Chinese roots and traditions.

"They don't want to become Western, they are proud to be Chinese. In this elite part of society, that is very important. But they also want to be welcomed and respected in the international community," Rue de Bernadac, known as Gill to his regular clients, says during a break in the afternoon's lessons.

"If you go to America or Australia and you have a business dinner at a high-end place, you want to know how to order."

While there are other foreign teachers in China, Rue de Bernadac is unusual as he is the only one who has broken into the market without a local partner. (Australia's etiquette queen June Dally-Watkins has a joint venture with a Chinese businessman.) The native Parisian practices what he preaches. He is the epitome of style, dressed in a double-breasted suit, with a red cravat and matching pocket square.

Etiquette training goes back four generations in Rue de Bernadac's family. His grandmother and her father were private tutors at the court of the King of Morocco for decades from the 1920s, a time when the African country was opening up to the West in the same way China has this century. He and his brother were schooled in good manners by their grandmother as children. He says they were not allowed to have dessert if they did not sit up straight at the dinner table. This was determined by whether a piece of paper tucked under each armpit remained in place throughout the meal.

After studying business and making an initial foray to China in 2011, he returned in 2014 to found the Academie de Bernadac in Shanghai, which also works with luxury brands and trains hospitality staff. About 95 per cent of his students are women but a growing number are sending their husbands and sons to classes. He says many of his clients are businesswomen not just bored housewives with wealthy husbands.

"We don't have many housewives who don't work. Most of them, like these ladies are businesswomen who are successful in their own way. They have a strong will to become a better person."

Rue de Bernadac's two other students that afternoon definitely fit the high-achieving category. Chu Mingjingjing, a Shanghai luxury brand ambassador dressed stylishly in a 1920s Chinese qipao, and jewellery designer Angela Chen, both grew up in Shanghai and hardly seem in need of etiquette lessons.

Chen, who was educated in Canada, says that she ended up in one of Rue de Bernadac's classes accidentally after originally sending her 14-year-old son to study European-style etiquette.

"My son was so busy at that time so I came to the class instead. I learnt a lot. I am from a Shanghainese family and I learnt table manners from my grandmother when I was a child. But while I went to university in British Columbia and Shanghai is a Western-style city, there were huge cultural differences when I went abroad," says Chen, who launched her jewellery label Angela Jewels six years ago.

"The fashion culture was different. We drink baijiu [Chinese liquor], you drink beer and red wine. I thought we should learn something. My son wanted to study in Britain or the US so sooner or later he would have to learn Western-style manners."

Chu, who started a luxury branding company called Luxe China, regularly mixes with royalty in Europe including Italy's Princess Catherine Colonna de Stigliano. Her family owned a publishing house before Mao Zedong's Communist Party ruled China in 1949 and grew up on the Bund. While the style and class of Shanghai in the 1930s disappeared during the Cultural Revolution, she says that it is making a comeback.

"I remember in Hong Kong and Taiwan, I saw the most elegant older ladies in their 80s and 90s. They have this nobility, they were naturally elegant, very classy, very well-dressed. They have experienced the best part of China in the 1930s, and this is something to preserve."

The surge in the number of middle class Chinese travelling overseas or sending their children to foreign universities has also triggered an interest in Western culture. But the main driver is money.

There were 1893 individuals in China with a fortune of 2 billion yuan ($420 million) or more last year, according to the annual Huran Rich List. This included 620 billionaires measured in US dollars, a six-fold increase from a decade ago. But while money may not be able to buy taste, it can apparently buy manners in China. A two-day group class ranges from 4000 yuan per day to 7900 yuan per person. One-on-one classes start at 12000 yuan per day. Business groups range from 12000 yuan for an afternoon to 30000 yuan for a day.

The posture lesson has now moved on and Rue de Bernadac is showing the ladies how to sit to make their legs look longer or slimmer. The secret is crossing your legs on the cuff. Where to place your hands?

"Place your hand on your wrist so you don't have big hands," he says

Tackling high tea also turns out to be a minefield. Fingers are allowed if whatever you are picking up doesn't make your hands sticky. Dipping scones into your tea is strictly forbidden. Start from salty to sweet, and work your way from the bottom of the carousel to top. Napkins must be folded into a triangle with lipstick marks hidden inside.

His 45-minute afternoon tea class is ironically one of the most popular, even though drinking tea was traditionally a Chinese pastime. Private classes range from deportment, dining etiquette and public speaking.

All three ladies roll their eyes when I ask what they think of the Crazy Rich Asians movie and how this has affected the West's image of China's middle classes. They do not appear to think much of the movie, which lampoons the flamboyant wealth of a wealthy Singaporean Chinese family, but they know one of the actors.

"The People's Republic of China is still a new country. We have more than 5000 years of history but the country, this government is still new," Chen says, while stirring her tea "from 6 to 12 o'clock" as instructed earlier in the class.

"People are getting rich in a very short space of time in the last 20 years. Now people have money, but what about spirit and values? That's what people are looking for."W

These ladies have a strong will to become a better person. Guillaume Rue de Bernadac, coach

HEADLINE: Sellers secretly dropping prices
TEXT:
Real estate Reluctant buyers, looking for bargains, are pushing agents to adopt unorthodox strategies to stimulate demand, writes Duncan Hughes.

Desperate real estate agents are bolstering nervous buyers by secretly offering lower prices in a bid to boost auction attendances, sales, and prices that have been falling for months.

Real estate agents are dropping quoted property prices by between 10 per cent and 16 per cent to select buyers in the final days before an auction in a bid to generate greater interest, correspondence between real estate and buyers' agents has revealed.

Prestige properties in Melbourne's inner south-east advertised online for between $2.5 million and $2.75 million are being offered in targeted correspondence to possible buyers for between $2.3 million and $2.5 million instead, a difference of about 16 per cent.

Agents claim the offers are being made to stimulate demand in sluggish markets where auction attendance and clearance rates continue to tumble as market sentiment weakens.

"If a sales campaign is not doing well, the agents might drop the indicative price to bait a potential buyer," says Cate Bakos, a buyers' agent for Cate Bakos Property.

"Vendors feeling the heat might lower expectations and sell at a lower price. They contact the real estate agents who then call around potential buyers and their representatives to say it might worth coming along to the auction because they might see a lower reserve."

It is also a way to attract more than one offer, encourage bidding and, hopefully, push up the price, according to agents receiving the correspondence. The practice has emerged as auction numbers dwindle, with about 930 auctions last weekend compared to more than 2000 the same week a year ago.

Sellers' fear of not getting out before prices fall further - or FONGO - is contributing to their willingness to negotiate on price and terms, particularly those who bought recently and are facing the prospect of the property's market value falling below its purchase price.

Reserve Bank of Australia analysis reveals what can happen when "irrational exuberance" turns to "irrational pessimism" in a housing market, even with record unemployment and record-low interest rates.

The central bank has calculated that, if home owners adjust their 10-year expected real house price gain from 2.5 per cent per year to zero, then real house prices could fall by a third over five years.

Amid rising anxiety over property prices, agents are attempting to bolster the market with pre-auction deals. Some of the properties they are discounting include:

*A four-bedroom, three-bathroom, two-storey Victorian mansion in landscaped gardens in Kew, about six kilometres east of Melbourne, being touted for between $10 million and $11 million is being offered to some buyers at a revised $9.8 million.

*The price of a single-storey house in Toorak has been discreetly reduced from an upper reserve of about $3.3 million to between $2.9 million and $3.1 million, despite the higher price still being advertised.

Sellers are also more likely to "meet the market", which might involve lowering their reserve price to secure a sale.

Real estate agent Rhonda Yim of Belle Property sold a three-bedroom property in Lewisham, in Sydney's inner-west, for $1,292,500, slightly less than the reserve of $1.3 million. She says sellers who believe their property has been marketed properly and attracted several potential buyers are willing to be pragmatic.

"There are others who have made some money from a property, particularly investors, who believe now is the right time to sell because of growing negative sentiment," Yim says. "But there are no signs of panic."

Emma Bloom, director of buyers' agent Morrell and Koren, says vendors are getting the message that buyers are looking for value and won't pay over-inflated prices.

"Some of these discounts are making the property prices fair and reasonable. It is where they should have been quoting in the first place," Bloom says.

Rich Harvey, chief executive of Sydney-based propertybuyer.com.au, says he is "not seeing much evidence" of FONGO. "I am not seeing any panicking or evidence of vendors having to get out of the market," he says.

Harvey says a powerful mix of falling prices and market uncertainty, particularly in the lead-up to the next federal election, is a great time to do a deal.

Buyers need to focus on the long-term fundamentals like location, amenity and value, adds Chris Foster-Ramsay, a mortgage broker for Foster Ramsay Finance.

There are plenty of properties selling well despite the doom and gloom, according to agents.

But Bloom warns transparent public auctions, where bidders can respond to counter-bids, are different from private negotiations, secret bids or round robins.

"Buyers need to know what to ask and what they are doing," says Bloom.

For example, she recommends buyers insist on seeing written evidence of any competing bids.

She claims real estate agents will attempt to keep buyers in the dark about the price and the number of bidders and sellers' readiness to do a deal. Too many buyers mistakenly think that when making a pre-auction offer, theirs will be the only offer presented to the vendor, says Bakos.

As public auction clearance rates continue to fall, boardroom auctions, round robins and "best and brightest" are becoming more popular.

Boardroom auctions involve competing buyers meeting in a room, typically an agent's boardroom, and bidding against each other.

Meeting face-to-face limits the risk of bluffing over the number of other bidders or their intentions. "I like them because they are transparent. Vendors still get the benefit of stimulated action," says Bakos.

But it is important to check any terms and conditions. For example, cooling-off periods might not be available. Sellers might also not accept conditional offers that make the bid subject to finance or the buyer selling their existing property.

Round robins are usually by phone, or by an agent communicating between bidders. The assumption is the winning bidder will sign the sale contract. But the successful bidder is not legally bound until the deal is signed. Buyers are usually relying on the integrity of the agent in being the go-between. "This can create distrust," says Bakos.

She says it is important for bidders to remember the selling agents are acting on behalf of the vendor to get them the highest price. A "best and brightest" sales approach involves a secret ballot where buyers are set the same deadline to submit their "best and highest" offer.

But there's an inherent lack of transparency in that method, and buyers - who do not like guessing prices in the first place - may end up offering too much.SI

If a sales campaign is not doing well, the agents might drop the indicative price. Cate Bakos, Cate Bakos Property

HEADLINE: How to ferret out a perfectly managed apartment block
TEXT:
With consumer confidence in new or off-the-plan apartments taking a hit after the Opal Tower crisis in Sydney, many potential purchasers are turning to established apartment blocks as a safer option.

Basically, you want a well-managed building: everything else flows from that. But how do you find this unicorn of an apartment block?

The obvious answer is to avoid the bad ones (d'uh!) and to do that, first look for clear signs that the building isn't being properly looked after.

Security and fire doors chocked open would be on your checklist, as well as furniture and other goods stored randomly in parking spaces or, even worse, fire stairwells.

Overflowing bins, cars parked permanently in visitor parking, and broken or missing lights in communal areas are also sure signs of systemic neglect.

Less obvious but even more worrying are lifts that don't quite line up with the floor and rattle and clatter as they move. That's an expensive issue just waiting to drop in your lap. Remember, as an owner you will be responsible for a share of all repairs and maintenance, so don't be the last player in a game of pass the buck.

Still interested? Now you want a forensic search done of the building's committee and general meeting minutes. A good, experienced strata lawyer or conveyancer will know what to look for, but they have to be prepared to read between the lines.

One dog-owning Flat Chat website reader was caught out when her pre-sale strata search failed to notice that, although there was a pet-friendly bylaw in place, there had been discussions about changing it to a more restrictive model.

By the time she moved in, the new bylaw was in place and she was told to get rid of her dog. The situation was eventually resolved but not without a lot of avoidable angst.

There are, however, more obvious warning signs. For instance, a lack of committee meetings is generally not good. That said, the smaller the building the fewer meetings required - in a two-storey walk-up, a lot of the day-to-day can be handled in lift-lobby chats.

However, any block of 50 or more units should be having meetings once a month. By the way, the legislation in most states only demands a general meeting, the AGM, once a year. The frequency of committee confabs is not legislated.

Other danger signs are perfunctory committee minutes that basically take the agenda and add the words "discussed", "defeated" or "agreed" to the motions. Or there are the great sweeping novels that name, blame and bully every individual with whom the chair or secretary disagrees.

Be wary of blocks where nothing contentious is ever recorded by the committee. No building has no problems, so no reference to any issues can mean they either aren't being dealt with or they are being covered up (or both).

More reassuring are minutes that reveal problems that have been or are currently being resolved. You also want to make sure the 10-year capital works plan has been properly devised and updated, and that money has been set aside to pay for repairs and upgrades as they arise.

A lively noticeboard and, even better, a regular newsletter is a good sign of an active and engaged committee and community. Tick all of the above boxes (and a physical checklist is worth compiling) and you may have found the epitome of a well-managed block. Good luck!SI

Jimmy Thomson edits the strata living advice website, flat-chat.com.au. States have different strata laws.

Be wary of blocks where nothing contentious is ever recorded by the committee.

HEADLINE: Why will industry funds benefit from Labor's franking proposals?John Wasiliev superquestions@afr.com
TEXT:
Exactly why, under Labor's proposed dividend imputation franking changes, are members of industry funds expected to be better off (from a tax perspective) than members of other types of super funds? Why should the higher ratios of accumulation to pension-phase accounts in industry funds be relevant if dividends and franking credits are strictly apportioned according to account type? Or are industry funds planning to transfer otherwise "lost" franking credits from pension account holders to accumulation account holders? Do any such transfers occur now in pooled super funds?

- Marie

A: There are a number of major industry funds that will not be materially affected by Labor's proposed removal of refunds for excess imputation credits. These industry funds - which like all super funds are taxpayers - have a net tax payable position even after the offset of imputation credits, says Sharon Osborn, of Focus Superannuation Services.

In other words they still pay more tax after deductions and credits. It is this tax payable position that will allow them to continue to receive the full benefit of dividend imputation tax credits and pass these to members reflected within their earnings.

Like other super funds, including self-managed funds, the funds will still have to gross up the share dividends they receive and add them to their income before deducting any expenses and tax credits.

The relevance of pooled or unsegregated funds having higher ratios of accumulation members - that can be as high as nine to one - is the level of tax liabilities they generate.

These tax liabilities result from accumulation members being liable to pay 15 per cent on all tax concessional super contributions from compulsory employer contributions or personal salary sacrifice contributions and the 15 per cent tax on their investment earnings.

There are other factors, but these liabilities contribute to the fund being able to offset in full the dividend imputation credits from share investment in their portfolios.

Before the declaration of investment earning rates or unit prices for any asset class such as Australian shares, part of the calculation is the application of the relevant tax rates, dividends and the attached imputation credits. The tax rate that is to be applied for accumulation member investment earnings is 15 per cent, although these members will also receive benefits from some other offsets that slightly reduces that actual rate. The proportion of earnings that apply to pension members reflects the zero tax earnings environment that such members are entitled to.

All industry super funds operate under tax laws and have internal tax management and governance frameworks that must be strictly adhered to. There are serious consequences should any fund manipulate the allocation of imputation credits to benefit one member over another.

That said, there may be a number of smaller industry funds that do not have a tax payable position and are currently receiving the benefit from excess imputation credits. For these funds, should Labor win government, their members will be affected with slightly lower earnings. If members are concerned about this they should contact their fund and ask if their super will lose net imputation refunds.

I have a query about the impact of the proposed Labor dividend imputation changes on investments in capital notes. In a previous article, it was stated that franking change will have the effect of removing the 30 per cent franking credit from the margin (referred to as the coupon rate) of a bank hybrid and not the bank bill rate (BBR) that is added to the margin. It uses the example of a NAB 4 per cent capital note (the NABPF). Is this correct? The prospectus for this investment states the franking credit is applied to both the margin and the BBR.

- Jim

A: Thank you for pointing this out, Jim. The franking credit adjustment is applied to both the coupon and the bank bill rate and not just the coupon, acknowledges John Likos, director of equity and credit research at Morningstar Australasia.

As an example, he illustrates what might happen if the latest capital notes by NAB were issued under Labor's proposed changes. The NAB hybrid (NABPF) offers a 4 per cent issue margin plus the bank bill swap rate, currently around 1.85 per cent. It was 2 per cent in the first answer.

The cash distribution is calculated by adding the issuer margin of 4 per cent to the bank bill swap rate of 1.85 per cent and then multiplying this by 70 per cent or (1-tax rate (30 per cent)).

What the Labor franking change will have the effect of doing, he says, is removing the 30 per cent cash rebate, or franking credit, received at tax time. This will reduce the distribution from 6.0 per cent to 4.1 per cent. So using a BBSR of 1.85 per cent and the stated margin of 4 per cent, the distribution would be (1.85% + 4.00%) x (1 - 0.30) = 4.10 per cent.

That said, there will be investors who will benefit from partial franking who can expect to earn returns of between 4.1 per cent and 6 per cent from an investment like the NAB hybrid. If the investor was an SMSF, for instance, it would need to have an accumulation account with a tax liability to benefit from partial franking.SI

John Wasiliev is a veteran writer on superannuation.

HEADLINE: Hold on to your assets for aged care choice
TEXT:
Expert view Don't be in a rush to cash in your superannuation and give it away to your children, writes Louise Biti.

Aged care is shaping up to be one of this year's hot topics with a royal commission under way into quality and safety, and as we head towards a federal election.

Medical and dietary advancements are enabling us to live longer, which is good news, but living longer also increases the chances that we will live through periods of frailty, either physical or mental, and require care to help with our day-to-day life.

In 2017, 3.8 million Australians were over the age of 65, representing about 15 per cent of the population. By 2057, 22 per cent of the population is expected to be over the age of 65.

Of this age group, just over 1 million people accessed a government subsidised aged care service either at home or in a residential care service during 2016-17. Usage increases with age, with 70 per cent of people aged 85 and over accessing subsidised care services.

With an ageing population, it is not surprising that there is more attention on ensuring our aged care system is able to provide quality care while remaining sustainable.

The ongoing cost of care is significantly subsidised by the federal government. In 2016-17, the federal government spent $17.1 billion on aged care services. This compares with $4.8 billion paid by consumers for access to those services.

How much a person pays towards the cost of care depends on affordability and financial means.

For example, a full age pensioner with no assets other than the family home who moves into residential aged care will need to pay for their room plus $50.66 per day ($18,491 per year) towards the cost of their care. Other incidentals may also apply.

The government may pay up to an additional $249.93 per day ($91,224 per year) to cover the rest of the care costs.

A self-funded retiree with a significant level of assets is likely to pay a means-tested fee, bringing the cost of care to an average across the year of up to $125.27 per day ($45,723 per year).

The government will still subsidise the costs, but at a lower rate. So where is the incentive to save your money to fund aged care needs if it only means you will be asked to pay more?

Many people think the answer is to start divesting assets to their children and rely on the government paying a greater share of the costs.

But don't be too hasty to cash in your superannuation and give it away to the children.

You could view the situation in the same way as you consider the decision to pay for private health insurance. For example, if you need a hip replacement this can be covered under Medicare, but you may have a long wait and will need to accept whichever doctor is allocated to you.

You may also have restricted choices for ongoing care and support. However, if you have private health insurance you maintain greater control and choice and may have a greater chance of getting the care you want, where and when you want.

We can't access private health insurance to cover aged care services, so the key to maintaining choice and control is to plan ahead. Decide what is important to you and understand what this may cost.

Then seek advice to plan how to structure and use your finances to help you fund access to these services. And don't start handing out inheritances before you are really done with your money.

While access to higher financial resources may increase your contribution towards the cost of your care, it may also increase the choices you have. It may allow you to pay for extra care services to top up the basic services provided.

Or it may allow you to choose a service provider that offers a higher standard of care or range of services. Or it may allow you to fund enough care services to remain in the home or other private accommodation arrangement.

Keeping and using your finances wisely keeps you in greater control over the quality of life you can maintain, even throughout periods of frailty.SI

Louise Biti is director of Aged Care Steps.

Where is the incentive to save your money to fund aged care needs if it only means you will be asked to pay more?

HEADLINE: WHAT SHORTEN COULD LEARN FROM KEATING
TEXT:
Former Treasury secretary Ted Evans talks Trump, the banking royal commission and the failure of Canberra to push through economic reforms with John Kehoe.

Ted Evans. Son of a fitter and turner. Left high school aged 15. Former Treasury secretary. Friend of Paul Keating. Former Westpac chairman. Today, my lunch companion.

Evans, 78 and now retired, walks past the bar at Walsh's Hotel in his hometown of Queanbeyan on the outskirts of Canberra. He lives just a few blocks away with his second wife, Judith, and their dog, and attends church nearby. It's just after midday and the locals are enjoying a drink here, at the town's first pub opened in 1885.

A scattering of patrons are in for lunch.

Evans, like me, spent about four years living in Washington DC - he at the International Monetary Fund about 30 years ago, me at the Australian Financial Review's bureau until last year.

"I think Trump might work out pretty well, actually," Evans says. "Having the nerve to do things like North Korea."

We nestle into a corner table at the adjoining Michael's restaurant, in a quiet room with wooden-topped tables and walls adorned with historic photos of the area.

For over two hours we discuss the lessons from the banking royal commission, the exasperating state of politics, the downfall of his old mate Ken Henry and the failure of Canberra to push through major economic reforms since Evans' glory days at Treasury during the Hawke, Keating and Howard governments.

"Keating was the best treasurer I've seen by a country mile," Evans declares. "He did so much with [prime minister Bob] Hawke's help. The whole of the '80s and to a lesser extent the '90s were really great for economic policy."

Evans still speaks regularly to Keating and recently saw him in Sydney at the launch of David Morgan: An Extraordinary Life, the biography of a fellow Treasury-cum-Westpac alumnus.

Evans joined Treasury in 1969 and was heavily involved in the reforms that underpinned a record 27 years of consecutive economic growth and higher living standards for Australians.

The sweeping overhaul included tax reforms, deregulating the financial system, increasing labour market flexibility and floating the currency.

When then secretary John Stone advised Keating against the currency float, Evans told the treasurer he disagreed with the Treasury boss.

Decades later when Evans retired as Westpac chairman, the bank arranged for television host Mike Munro to hold a special "This Is Your Life" ceremony with video messages from Evans' old mates from around the world, including Keating, who impersonated Stone's antics on the currency debate: "You disagree? You disagree, Ted? You disagree!" Keating rang out in the re-enactment.

Evans is a little hard of hearing and tells a story about his disobedient Cavoodle chewing up his hearing aid. I speak up.

The currency float in 1983 helped to pave the way for deregulating the labour market, Evans says. "Labour market reforms were the most important thing that needed to be done."

Inflation had hit 15 per cent in the 1970s and was still nudging double digits in the early '80s, as the centralised wage system drove up pay and prices.

Hawke introduced the prices and incomes accord and unions agreed to trade wage rises for superannuation. Later, prime minister John Howard broke the union stranglehold on the waterfront and extended enterprise bargaining and individual contracts. "That's why we've got so much better employment outcomes and a lower inflation rate," Evans says.

So what does he make of the Shorten Labor Opposition foreshadowing a generous rise in the minimum wage, possible reintroduction of pattern bargaining in low-wage industries and boosting union rights?

"I think that will be a problem and the start of our going backwards," he says. The consequences, he says, will be fewer jobs and higher inflation.

Evans' view is informed by personal experience. He left school in year 10 and joined the precursor to Telstra, the government-owned PMG, as a telecoms technician. While there, he completed school part-time and started a mathematics degree at Queensland University as an external student.

Then the unions negotiated a 25 per cent pay rise for PMG engineers and Evans became a casualty. "PMG responded by cutting out the cadetship," he says.

It was a brutal lesson in the realities of supply and demand in the labour market. Evans was forced to drop out of university but ultimately returned to study economics.

An encounter over a drink with leading academic economist Max Corden convinced him to forgo a PhD offer in New Zealand and to join Treasury in Canberra to learn some economics.

"As much as you learn the economic tools at university, your best learning is on the job and being involved in real issues."

The 28-year-old graduate with his second child on the way, to his first wife, Heather, was on a meteoric rise.

We peruse the menu and Evans warns the portions are very big. He opts for the battered flathead fillets. I choose the Porterhouse steak and order at the counter. Evans drinks water. He says he enjoys a nightly ritual of two 500ml cans of German non-alcoholic beer.

As Treasury deputy secretary in the '80s and '90s he worked very closely with Keating. He was secretary when Keating was prime minister and worked for treasurers John Dawkins, Ralph Willis and Peter Costello, between 1993 and 2001.

Evans had been parachuted into Canberra as Treasury secretary from Washington in 1993 after Tony Cole was let go by treasurer Dawkins.

Three years earlier Evans had suffered his first heart attack, at 49. Heart failure had claimed the life of his father at their Ipswich, Queensland, family home when Ted was 18 and also later killed his close friend treasury secretary Chris Higgins.

Evans considers himself lucky to have survived two heart attacks and has had bypass surgery, stents and a defibrillator.

He says Costello, now chairman of Nine - publisher of AFR Weekend -was highly intelligent and with Howard successfully introduced the overdue GST Hawke and Keating considered but infamously dropped at the eleventh hour.

So, why was Keating the best?

"He was a very quick learner. He had no economics training but listened very carefully and was just very determined. He pushed things through."

Could Labor's shadow treasurer Chris Bowen, who speaks to Keating most days, be a successful reformer like his idol?

"He's not showing any signs of being up to it, frankly," Evans says. "He doesn't speak enough on things that matter."

The softly spoken Evans had a fierce reputation for standing up to treasurers.

One behind-the-scenes encounter saw him stand up to John Howard on the importance of RBA independence by not publicly hinting at his preference for interest rate changes.

"I suspect it's not what it used to be like, [today]" he says in an oblique reference to the two most recent heads of Treasury, Philip Gaetjens and John Fraser, political appointments of the Coalition government.

Evans also laments that government-appointed advisory boards are not listened to. He recently chaired the ABC chair selection panel, which put forward four candidates, only for the government to appoint Ita Buttrose, who wasn't on the shortlist.

Speaking generally, he says: "Committees are really a charade." By the same token, he acknowledges bureaucrats don't have all the wisdom, including in financial markets and corporate tax.

It's why one of his proudest achievements was setting up the Board of Taxation to advise the government.

When he joined Westpac in 2001, Evans admits, "I was very embarrassed to find out how very little I knew about the operations of the financial markets."

Our meals arrive. "Oh, look at that," he says, as the super-sized fish and steak are placed on the table.

We shift our conversation to the banking royal commission. Evans joined the Westpac board in 2001 and became chairman in 2007 before retiring in 2011.

He admits he was surprised by the extent of problems exposed by the commissioner, Kenneth Hayne.

"I'd long been very concerned about the wage system in banking," Evans says. "The salaries are rather outlandish. Not chief executives', but those involved in markets where in most banks people are paid what they earn in the market using the bank's balance sheet. Some of it is good risk management, but most of it is just betting."

Westpac had a system of incentives to deter traders from using bank capital to make risky bets.

"Even so they'd make a mint. Some of our traders earned more than many of the executives," he says.

As a bank director, the challenge was that the international employment market inflated banker salaries, he says.

Evans looks at his plate and says he should stop picking at the pile of chips.

I ask what he makes of his former Treasury colleague Henry, who was recently forced to quit as National Australia Bank chairman after the commission's damning findings.

"I feel very sorry for him. I think the reaction was grossly overdone. He is an outstanding person in every sense."

Evans, Henry and Morgan worked closely on tax reform for Keating. "Ken was a great asset and model builder," Evans says.

Over cappuccinos we discuss Henry's successor at NAB, Phil Chronican, who was a chief financial officer at Westpac.

"He just understands economics extraordinarily well."

Evans passed over Chronican, Rob Whitfield and Phil Coffey for Westpac's top job in favour of Gail Kelly from St George.

"We were fortunate in Westpac to have an excellent CEO in Gail Kelly - the best public speaker I've ever seen."

As we prepare to exit, Evans says he now spends his days doing dozens of crosswords and Sudoku puzzles, plus Googling jokes to share with friends. "I love humour," he says as he gets into his white Lexus. W

HEADLINE: Strategies for dealing with Labor's changes
TEXT:
Investors should try to seal their property purchases before January 1 to lock in existing negative gearing tax breaks and capital gains tax discount rather than buy "riskier", newly built property under Labor's proposed tax reforms, say financial advisers.

Jonathan Philpot, a partner at accountants HLB Mann Judd, said investors still had time to acquire negatively geared existing property if they wanted to build their wealth that way.

"But they have to get their acts into gear now because it's a tougher process with the banks to get loans approved," he said.

Mr Philpot discouraged investors from holding off and investing in riskier, newly built property from January 1, which under Labor's policy can still be negatively geared but will only qualify for a 25 per cent CGT discount.

"New property has its own issues. If you look at the disasters in property investing, it does tend to be on the new side of things," he said.

Mr Philpot also advised against holding residential property in self-managed super funds - under Labor's proposed changes the reduced 25 per cent CGT discount won't apply to super funds - because of the weak 2-3 per cent returns they generated and the increased liquidity risks.

Property investment adviser Margaret Lomas said buying existing property before January 1 was "an absolute yes" for her.

"While I don't believe that tax benefits should be the driving force behind your decision to invest in property, the benefits that you can get from negative gearing are really helpful to your cash flows in the early years," said Ms Lomas.

"If you have the right kind of risk profile, and the bank will lend to you, and you have done what is required to become an educated investor, then I'd be buying as much as I could before the new rules come in."

Ms Lomas also discouraged investors holding off and buying new property from January 1.

"New property has always been a bad idea for property investors. It comes at a premium for starters, and while an owner-occupier might be happy to pay that premium for features, those same features rarely bring much additional rent return. A property a few years old has always been a better option than a brand new property."

Nerida Cole, head of advice at wealth managers Dixon Advisory, said it made sense for investors to hold onto growth assets (negatively geared or not) that benefited from the 50 per cent CGT concession.

"It's important to consider what the outlook for that asset is. If it's still a good growth prospect, like a blue-chip property or in a growing suburb, then you should hold onto it," she said.

Ms Cole said Labor's proposed changes to negative gearing, CGT and franking credits should encourage investors to examine their portfolios and consider which assets to hold long-term. In addition, she said all these changes highlighted the importance of "good record keeping".

"You need to make sure you have a good system in place to keep track which classes of shares (or property) were bought at which date, and the different tax consequences, of selecting one over another if you want to free up cash."

Simon Cohen, founder of Sydney buyer's agents Cohen Handler, said a lot of their clients were already looking to buy to beat the proposed changes.

But investors should avoid rushed decisions. "The fear of something is always greater than the actual impact. You don't want to ... make a mistake."

HEADLINE: Lowest in 14 years
TEXT:
The proportion of Australia's 2.2 million landlords who are negatively geared fell to 60 per cent in fiscal 2017, the lowest since 2003, the latest Tax Office statistics show.

Investment properties that are negatively geared have diminished as interest rates have fallen. When losses on an investment property are greater than the gains, the losses can be used to reduce tax on wages or other income. Landlords claimed median net losses of $1427, down 9 per cent on the year before.

But if Labor is elected, it will end this arrangement on all properties except new ones from January 1, 2020.

Existing investments will be grandfathered and the 40 per cent of landlords who have positive or neutral gearing will not be affected. A parallel Labor policy to halve the capital gains tax discount will increase taxes on gains when investment properties are sold. Median capital gains reported by individuals rose a hefty 30 per cent.

JOANNA MATHER AND EDMUND TADROS

HEADLINE: Labor investor hit to favour big super
TEXT:
Labor's tax crackdown on real estate and dividend franking credits will push billions of dollars into big superannuation funds that will benefit from new tax breaks.

Union and employer controlled industry funds will be big winners from Labor's tax and super shake-ups, which will make it harder for individuals and self-managed superannuation funds (SMSFs) to invest in property.

Gene Tunny, principal at Canberra consultancy Adept Economics, said: "If Labor makes investing in property less attractive by restricting negative gearing then people will look to shift their money elsewhere and super may well be the best place to put it.

"That is particularly so given Labor will not reduce the capital gains tax (CGT) discount for super funds."

Property investors will consider racing to beat Labor's ban from January 1 2020 on negative gearing and cutting of the CGT discount in half to 25 per cent, announced by shadow treasurer Chris Bowen on Friday ahead of Tuesday's federal budget.

Existing investments made before the deadline and newly built homes in the future will be exempted from the proposed changes.

SQM Research managing director Louis Christopher said there was uncertainty over whether investors would embark on a late buying spree to seize on the last chance to negatively gear before the end of this year.

"It's going to be a fairly choppy market and tricky for investors to time their acquisition or sale," he said.

"It depends what the Reserve Bank of Australia does with interest rates and if investors see through the other side of any possible house price rally because prices will very likely fall away in the new year."

BIS Oxford Economics managing director Robert Mellor, who has seen five housing cycles in Sydney, said it was unlikely people would rush to buy property before the tax crackdown.

"At a time of falling house prices people won't jump in just because of tax breaks," he said.

"Investor lending is down and I don't think we will see the bottom of the market until next year."

Labor will also clamp down on leveraged property speculation by SMSFs by banning what is known as limited recourse borrowing after financial regulators raised risk concerns.

Big super funds on Friday were celebrating Mr Bowen's announcement that a future Labor government would boost the nascent build-to-rent sector by halving to 15 per cent the managed investment trust withholding tax rate for institutional investors who build new rental properties.

Industry super funds already investing in the build-to-rent sector offshore include Australian Super, First State and REST. They are poised to plough capital into the domestic rental market.

Chris Key managing director of the local arm of the world's largest build to rent provider Greystar, said Labor's change to a "punitive tax" will attract global capital and domestic super funds will follow.

"It unlocks global capital to invest in the asset class," he said.

"A lot of the local super funds have taken the view that they are not typically the first mover - they prefer to see the investment get proven."

The housing moves will help establish an institutionalised investment rental market like in the United States and United Kingdom, but come at the expense of mum and dad landlords.

As Sydney and Melbourne property prices continue to slide and housing credit growth fell to its lowest level since records began in 1977, new tax statistics on Friday showed 60 per cent of landlords recorded net rental income losses in 2016-17, the smallest share in 13 years.

The Morrison government and property industry said Labor's tax changes would put more downward pressure on home prices.

"Labor has finally revealed when their economy wrecking housing taxes will start - confirming that Labor simply doesn't care about the impact their housing taxes will have on Australians or countless experts

warning about the disastrous impact they will have on the economy," Assistant Minister for Treasury Zed Seselja said.

Mr Bowen said the latest Australian Taxation Office data showed that since 2014 the number of people who own four or five properties was growing at almost six times the rate of people who own one property.

He ruled out any delays to curbing property tax breaks if the downturn got worse.

"The policy we take to the election is the policy we will seek to implement," he said.

"It's in the best interest of first home-buyers.

"It's in the best interest of people who want to get involved in construction, either through build to rent or because we put our negative gearing policies to work by allowing new properties going forward."

If Labor wins the May federal election, it would likely have to negotiate the tax package through a hostile Senate.

The less favourable investment tax arrangements for individuals and SMSFs will be amplified by Labor's pledge to end the cash refund of $5.5 billion in annual dividend franking credits for people who pay little or no tax.

Shifting money out of SMSFs into better-returning big industry and retail funds could benefit many retirees.

SMSFs with less than $500,000 perform "significantly worse" on average than regular funds, the Productivity Commission has said.

However, SMSF Association chief John Maroney said Labor's confirmation of a July 1 2019 start date for abolishing franking credit rebates showed "total disregard for self-funded retirees."

"The association has always opposed Labor's proposal on the grounds it is iniquitous, discriminating against those retirees who have opted to manage their retirement savings through an SMSF while leaving many of those in APRA-regulated funds untouched - a clear violation of the sound policy principle of horizontal equity," he said.

"That these retirees will not have the certainty of legislation to allow them to restructure their affairs and, in many instances, be severely financially disadvantaged because of it, is simply unjust."

Almost $11 billion flowed out of scandal-plagued retail super funds into industry funds in 2018, with AustralianSuper the biggest winner and AMP the biggest loser, in the wake of the financial services royal commission's damning findings.

Grattan Institute policy fellow Brendan Coates said investing in superannuation funds would become marginally more attractive investments for most people, compared to property and SMSFs.

"Investors are very sensitive to different rates between investment vehicles and so you will see a shift away from vehicles that are taxed more heavily and towards those taxed more concessionally," he said.

HEADLINE: Investors look to sell in market that may not be business as usual
TEXT:
Investment homes Sydney's northern suburbs braced.

Nick Strong wasn't planning to sell his two-bedroom apartment in Lane Cove. He purchased it in 2004 for $370,000 and, since moving out, was happy to keep renting it.

"Even going into the market downturn, I had no intention of selling it. The market normally turns around and it's business as usual," Mr Strong said.

But he expects Labor to win the expected May election and - given the opposition's stated plan to implement its changes to negative gearing and capital gains tax from January 1 - that means the residential market in Sydney's northern suburbs is in for a change.

"Business may not be as per usual come the May election with Labor's intention to change laws around the tax and how its treated, on capital gains tax side and the negative gearing side," said Mr Strong, an insurance underwriter.

"They're going to essentially almost halve the market of potential buyers for existing rental properties."

The possible implementation of policies to limit negative gearing tax breaks to new, rather than established, homes, and to halve the capital gains tax deduction on investment property sales to 25 per cent could trigger a burst of buying by investors seeking to beat the changes and lock in existing tax savings, said CoreLogic research analyst Cameron Kusher.

"If Labor win the election there could be a bounce for investment purchasing second half of 2019 (and then a big pullback early 2020)," Mr Kusher said.

At the other end of the Hume Highway in Melbourne's St Kilda, Hockingstuart agent Sam Inan said Labor's plans would make wealthy investors who wanted to offset the tax losses from owning high-quality investment homes against their other income rush into property. "This will propel them more quickly," he said.

Mr Strong's 88-96 Helen Street apartment goes on the market on Monday and he's hoping for about $750,000. That's less than the unit's $860,000 valuation a year and a half ago, but he wants to get out ahead of the fall in the residential market he expects Labor's policies to trigger. "It's not the best time to sell," he said. "If I had sold a year ago I would be happier. But because I have held it so long, it's just reducing in profit, it's not negative equity."

Agent Patrick Lang of Belle Property Lane Cove said the actual implementation of any new policy is uncertain even if Labor takes power in the House of Representatives, as it will depend on the make-up of the Senate. Even so, the property market is in for a hit, he said

There are about 75 units currently on the market in Lane Cove, in the heart of Sydney's northern suburbs, less than the 120-odd that marked a high level of supply and one that would normally mean a strong level of competition. However, supply is not the problem.

"Supply seems to be fine," Mr Lang said. "It's demand levels that are underpinning our micro-market."

Mr Strong, who currently rents his own home, said he would not look to buy in the current market. He'll wait it out.

"Initially, I'll be putting money into investment uses," he said. "Where I can see good solid return, I'll save, sit back and see what happens to the market following the rules."
